lead: A Cauchy sequence is a list of real numbers whose terms become close to each other, not necessarily close to a known limit. The idea exists because many convergence proofs need a test that does not name the limit. In ℝ, every Cauchy sequence has a real limit; this is completeness. Only a few universities teach this topic. Numerical methods and series tests use it to prove that approximations settle down.
prereq: You need: convergence of sequences from 3.1, series and partial sums from 3.2, and absolute value inequalities.

blocks.text: The definition asks the terms to crowd together. For every real ε > 0 there is an integer N such that |a_m − a_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N. Here ε is the allowed gap; N depends only on ε, never on m or n. The sequence is a_n, and |x| is absolute value.
Every convergent sequence is Cauchy. If a_n → L, choose N so |a_n − L| < ε/2 for n ≥ N. For m, n ≥ N, the triangle inequality gives |a_m − a_n| ≤ |a_m − L| + |L − a_n| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε.

The converse is deeper. In ℝ it is true: every Cauchy sequence converges. In ℚ it can fail, as Section 2 shows. The Cauchy condition is limit-free, but it certifies convergence only when the space has no gaps.

Completeness of ℝ has an equivalent form: every nonempty set of real numbers bounded above has a least upper bound, called the supremum. The supremum is the smallest real number ≥ every element. This property fills all gaps in the line.
The Archimedean property follows: for every real x there is a natural number n with n > x. It lets 1/n be made smaller than any chosen ε. For example, to force 2/N < ε = 0.01, you need N > 200.
The rationals ℚ have gaps. Decimal truncations of √2, such as 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, …, are rational and Cauchy, but their limit √2 is irrational. So they have no limit in ℚ.

The Cauchy criterion for series: Σ a_n converges if and only if its partial sums are Cauchy. Equivalently, for every ε > 0 there is N such that |a_{N+1} + … + a_m| < ε for all m > N. This tests a series without finding its sum.

figure.caption: The solid path shows a Cauchy sequence (ε = 0.01) whose limit L exists in ℝ; the second solid step is the completeness of ℝ that guarantees L. The dashed path shows the same construction failing in ℚ at √2.

spec.aria: A Cauchy sequence gets a real limit because ℝ is complete; a dashed branch shows the rational gap at √2.

examples.question: Show that a_n = 1/n is Cauchy. For ε = 0.01, find an N that satisfies the definition, and verify the bound at that N.
steps: Take m, n ≥ N with N a positive integer. Since m, n ≥ N > 0, 1/m ≤ 1/N and 1/n ≤ 1/N.
Take N = 201, the smallest integer greater than 200. Then 2/N = 2/201 ≈ 0.00995 < 0.01.
For all m, n ≥ 201, |1/m − 1/n| ≤ 2/201 < 0.01. Hence a_n is Cauchy; in ℝ it converges to 0.
examples.answer: The choice N = 201 makes |1/m − 1/n| ≤ 2/201 ≈ 0.00995 < 0.01 for all m, n ≥ 201, so a_n = 1/n is Cauchy.
examples.check:
eps = 0.01
bound = 2 / eps
N = int(bound) + 1
bound_at_N = 2 / N
print(eps)
print(bound)
print(N)
print(round(bound_at_N, 5))

traps: Saying Cauchy implies convergence in every ordered field. It fails in ℚ; completeness is a property of ℝ.
Choosing N after seeing m and n. N may depend on ε only and must work for all m, n ≥ N.
Confusing the series Cauchy criterion with the term test. Terms tending to 0 is necessary, not sufficient.
Claiming the rational truncations of √2 converge in ℚ. They converge in ℝ to irrational √2.

quiz.q: State the Cauchy condition for a_n.
quiz.a: For every ε > 0 there is N such that |a_m − a_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

quiz.q: Why is every convergent sequence Cauchy?
quiz.a: If a_n → L, take N with |a_n − L| < ε/2 for n ≥ N. For m, n ≥ N, |a_m − a_n| ≤ |a_m − L| + |L − a_n| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε.

quiz.q: For a_n = 1/n and ε = 0.02, find N using |1/m − 1/n| ≤ 2/N.
The rationals 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … are Cauchy. Why no limit in ℚ?
quiz.a: Their limit is √2, which is irrational. ℚ has a gap there, so no rational L is the limit.

quiz.q: State the least upper bound property of ℝ.
quiz.a: Every nonempty set of reals bounded above has a least upper bound, called the supremum.

quiz.q: Does a_n → 0 imply Σa_n satisfies the Cauchy criterion? Explain with the harmonic series.
quiz.a: No. In the harmonic series the block a_{N+1}+…+a_{2N} ≥ 1/2, so partial sums are not Cauchy although a_n → 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same idea defines complete metric spaces and Banach spaces in functional analysis. Numerical analysis uses Cauchy sequences to prove iterative methods settle even when the limit is unknown. Search “Cauchy sequence Banach space” and “construction of real numbers by Cauchy sequences”.
